title: Combination Sum II
description:
You are given a list `candidates` of positive integers, possibly with repeated values, and a target sum `target`. Find every unique combination of candidates adding up to `target`, where **each position in the list can be used at most once**.

Two combinations that contain the same values (as a multiset) are duplicates and only one of them may be returned. Order of the output does not matter.

examples.explanation: There are two 1s in the input, so [1,1,6] is valid, but [1,7] must appear only once even though either 1 could be used.

hints: Sort the candidates so that equal values are adjacent and you can prune once a value exceeds the remaining sum.
Recurse with start = i + 1 (each position once). To avoid duplicate multisets, skip candidates[i] if it equals candidates[i-1] and i > start.
Use `break` rather than `continue` when candidates[i] > remaining: the list is sorted, so nothing after it fits either.
signature: def combinationSum2(self, candidates: List[int], target: int) -> List[List[int]]:
approach:
**Key insight: combine the two standard tricks, sorted-break pruning from Combination Sum and same-depth duplicate skipping from Subsets II.** Each position is used once, so the recursive call advances to `i + 1`.

**Algorithm.** Sort. `backtrack(start, remaining)`: record on `remaining == 0`. Loop `i` from `start`; `break` if `candidates[i] > remaining`; `continue` if `i > start` and `candidates[i] == candidates[i-1]`; otherwise push, recurse on `(i + 1, remaining - candidates[i])`, pop.

**Why it works.** Sorting makes the break valid and makes duplicates adjacent. The skip rule ensures that among equal values, the combination always takes a prefix of the run, so each multiset has one canonical path.

**Common mistakes:** checking the skip rule before the break (still correct but order the cheap prune first); writing `i > 0` instead of `i > start`, which wrongly forbids using two equal values in the same combination; forgetting that the input `[1]*20 + [2]*20` explodes without dedup.

**Interview follow-ups:** Why is the `[1]*20 + [2]*20` style input the real test of your solution? (without the skip rule you explore 2^40 branches.) How does the complexity compare to Combination Sum? (depth bounded by n here, by target/min there.) Could a counting approach (value -> frequency) be cleaner? (yes: iterate distinct values and choose how many copies to take, 0..freq.)
